title: Heme & Endo Exam 3 Hub
examInfo: Exam 3: 35 multiple-choice questions on new material only: Dr. Taylor's Lecture A and L17-L22. Nothing from Exam 1 or Exam 2's lectures.
Friday, November 20, 8:00-9:30 am (the dental students' sitting; optometry sits at 10:00).
In person, Volker Hall Lecture Room B, on Canvas with LockDown Browser, as for Exams 1 and 2.

A Dental endocrinology clinical application (Dr. Taylor), L17 Pregnancy and lactation (Dr. Madison), L18 Estrogens and androgens (Dr. Fasinu), L19 Introduction to hematology (Dr. Herr), L20 Lymphomas and leukemias (Dr. Borak), L21 and L22 Pathology of the male and female reproductive systems (Dr. Dal Zotto).

There's no in-class review for Exam 3: Dr. Herr gave a study guide instead (November 17), with the points to focus on and the key terms for L17 to L22. Everything on it is a High Likelihood question in this hub, and its lists open each lecture's Exam Hints.
Dr. Taylor's lecture was taught November 6 but left off Exam 2 (Dr. Herr said he forgot it), so it moved to Exam 3 with everything the Exam 2 hub had for it.

Of the 35: Lecture A (Clinical application) 3, L17 Pregnancy and lactation 4, L18 Estrogens and androgens 6, L19 Introduction to hematology 8, L20 Lymphomas and leukemias 6, L21 Male reproductive pathology 4 and L22 Female reproductive pathology 4. The mock follows the same counts.
Quiz 4 is due Thursday, November 19, at 11:59 pm. This hub uses nothing from the quizzes or the take-home.

lectures.title: Male Reproductive and Lower Urinary Tract Pathology

likelyTopics.t: Hypoglycemia in the chair: the signs, a finger-stick (some CGMs stop reading at a floor), straight glucose rather than table sugar, a slow response on a GLP-1 drug, glucagon IM or subcutaneously if oral glucose fails

Before treating a diabetic: HbA1c above 7 is poorly controlled (implant failure, periodontal disease), confirm the meal and medication, morning appointments; Dr. Taylor's metformin with a skipped breakfast; pack-years
Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease (his first case): epinephrine caution, and thyroid storm (fever, pulse 140 or more; call 911)
Addison disease (his third case): oral pigment from high ACTH, adrenal crisis triggers and signs, extra corticosteroid after a big procedure; Cushing syndrome and long-term steroids
Hyperparathyroidism on the radiograph (lost lamina dura, radiolucent brown tumors, mobility) and the calcium regulators (PTH, vitamin D, calcitonin)
Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing
The three hormone classes with examples, receptors, and endocrine versus nervous signaling
Diabetes: type 1 versus type 2 (insulin ineffective, not deficient), oral manifestations and the sugar in saliva, the two-way periodontal link, SGLT2 drugs and UTIs
Hyperthyroid versus hypothyroid dental considerations (hypothyroidism far more common), and the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery
Sex hormones and the mouth: puberty, pregnancy gingivitis and the interproximal pyogenic granuloma, menopause
Pituitary hormones (ADH and diabetes insipidus), alpha and beta cells, and the adrenal medulla

hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone (the hormone that readies the endometrium) and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures

Prolactin versus oxytocin: prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down through the myoepithelial cells; during pregnancy progesterone antagonizes prolactin, so full milk production waits for delivery
Suckling's neuroendocrine effects: dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin; suckling lowers dopamine and raises oxytocin from the posterior pituitary; prolactin inhibits GnRH, so periods stop

Delivery and after: the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio rises; uterine distention, prostaglandins (PGF2 alpha for contraction, PGE2 for the cervix) and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary drive labor; oxytocin limits bleeding after delivery

The placenta takes over the steroids: estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetal adrenal's 17,20 desmolase and the fetal liver before its aromatase makes estriol
The placenta's other hormones: human placental lactogen opposes insulin (an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic pregnancy and gestational diabetes); relaxin keeps the uterus quiet
The placenta as an organ: what it makes (hCG, hPL, relaxin, progesterone, estriol; not oxytocin) and what crosses it
Building the breast for milk: estrogen grows and branches the ducts, progesterone adds the alveoli, prolactin and cortisol raise the milk enzymes
The endocrine basis of contraception: the pill blunts the LH surge, progestin thickens the cervical mucus, high-dose estrogen prevents implantation
Fertilization: ZP3 sets off the acrosomal reaction, the sperm then binds ZP2, the oocyte finishes its second meiotic division, and the cortical reaction blocks polyspermy
Implantation at the blastocyst stage: trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts (nurse cells) versus syncytiotrophoblasts (invasion), and decidualization
Capacitation: why ejaculated sperm can't fertilize yet, and the membrane changes that make the acrosomal reaction possible
Maternal hormones that promote fertilization: estrogen at ovulation helps the sperm, then holds the embryo back until progesterone relaxes the myometrium

GnRH analogs: the body releases GnRH in pulses, but a long-acting analog (goserelin, leuprolide) stimulates the pituitary continuously until it switches off LH, FSH and testosterone; mainly prostate cancer; anti-sex-hormone side effects

Blocking androgen metabolism and receptors: the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors finasteride and dutasteride (Proscar and Propecia are one drug; his finasteride dental case) and the receptor antagonists flutamide and bicalutamide

How hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy: progestins activate the progestin receptor and suppress FSH and LH, so no ovulation; ethinyl estradiol in the combined pill; progestin-only pills (levonorgestrel) when estrogen is ruled out

Thromboembolism, the estrogens' most serious side effect: more clotting factors and less antithrombin III; shared by the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors (his raloxifene dental case); oral anticoagulants work less well; any clot, even years ago, rules estrogen out

Testosterone's adverse effects and cautions: hepatotoxicity (the most important), virilization in women, feminization in men, lower HDL, the gel at bedtime, and when to avoid it (BPH, pregnancy, breast cancer in men)

Emergency contraception and the anti-progestins: Plan B (levonorgestrel, 72 hours, no prescription) versus ulipristal (a progestin receptor antagonist, 5 days, prescription); mifepristone also blocks glucocorticoid receptors
SERMs: why they are selective; tamoxifen (breast antagonist, uterine agonist, ER-positive tumors only), raloxifene for osteoporosis, clomiphene for ovulation
Aromatase inhibitors: anastrozole blocks testosterone's conversion to estradiol to treat breast cancer; hot flashes and thromboembolism; not before menopause
Testosterone's two fates: 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT, the active form, and aromatase makes estradiol (the tall, osteoporotic man without aromatase); DHEA, the over-the-counter precursor

What estrogen does and its side effects: female maturation and the endometrium, HDL and triglycerides up, bone protected, the skin (the pill for acne); fluid retention; oral estrogens act on the liver; progesterone added to protect the uterus
The estrogen drugs: estradiol from the ovary, ethinyl estradiol in oral contraceptives, estrone in Premarin for menopause; the indications

How the sex steroids act (nuclear receptors, carried on SHBG), what testosterone does (red cells, water retention, muscle) and the androgens' uses; testosterone cypionate, the depot; progesterone matures the endometrium

Recognizing the blood cells and their jobs: red cells (most of the cells) carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets come from megakaryocytes ("just knowledge you should know") and start clotting, and the white cells come in two classes and five types: the granulocytes and the agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes), each with its share, most to least common, its nucleus and its line in the hematopoiesis tree

The white cells' jobs: the neutrophil (multi-lobed, about 10 hours in the blood, the first line of defense against bacteria), eosinophil (red granules, major basic protein against parasites, allergy), basophil (dark blue granules, heparin, asthma) and monocyte (becomes the macrophage and expresses MHC II)

B and T cells: B cells carry surface IgM and IgD, and a B cell whose antibody fits an antigen recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell that releases that antibody, in a secondary organ; helper T cells (CD4, antigen on MHC II) help the B cells, cytotoxic T cells (CD8) kill what they bind, and T cells carry memory

NK cells: the large lymphocytes, with no B or T markers and no specific receptors; MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the inhibitory receptor and stops the killing, a cell missing it is killed, and too many activating ligands cause induced killing; CD16 binds IgG's constant region in ADCC, with macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils

Innate versus adaptive immunity: what the body just does (barriers, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate, interferons, phagocytes, NK cells), versus the antibodies of the humoral arm ("think B-cell response") and the T cells of the cellular arm

Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: the primary ones are just the bone marrow and the thymus (not GALT), where B and T cells become immunocompetent without antigen ("bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells"; self-reactive B cells removed in the marrow); every other one, lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and the spleen, is secondary

The spleen: the PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery ("associate this PALS with the spleen"); the splenic artery from the celiac trunk bringing blood-borne antigens in, with no afferent lymphatics; white pulp and red pulp; the marginal zone; red pulp of cords and sinusoids; and what the spleen does

The thymus: epithelioreticular cells form its stroma ("I do want you to know that"), reticular cells and type III collagen everywhere else; the dense, dark cortex versus the lighter medulla; the blood-thymus barrier's three layers; and involution to fat by the teens

The lymph node: the lymph's route (afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic); activation in the paracortex and follicles, B cells multiplying in germinal centers and plasma cells secreting antibody in the medulla; B cells in the follicles and T cells in the paracortex; dendritic and follicular dendritic cells; blood lymphocytes entering through high endothelial venules

T cell education: precursors in through postcapillary venules, out to the cortex, positive and negative selection, single CD4 or CD8 cells out to the secondary organs, and 95 to 99 percent selected out by apoptosis

The splenic sinuses and the blood's path: rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells with macrophage processes, strands of basal lamina at right angles, no smooth muscle and no pericytes; in the open circulation, sheathed capillaries empty into the cords

MALT and the tonsils: Peyer's patches in the ileum, under M cells that take microbes from the lumen; the pharyngeal, tubal (at the auditory tube), palatine and lingual tonsils, and the crypts that trap material; IgA into the lumen, and adenoiditis
Classifying the leukemias on two axes: acute (blasts that don't mature) or chronic (cells that still mature), and myeloid or lymphoid: AML, ALL, CML and CLL

Acute versus chronic leukemia (onset, course, blasts, platelets, organomegaly) and leukemia's clinical consequences: marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, infection) and cells growing in tissues (bone pain, spleen, liver, nodes, and the gums, where a dentist may be the first clue)

Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin: Hodgkin is usually localized, spreads contiguously, rarely leaves the nodes and never involves the blood, with a few large Reed-Sternberg cells; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is usually widespread, can skip node groups, often starts outside the nodes, can reach the blood, and is mostly B-cell

AML's diagnostic threshold (more than 20 percent blasts; any count with a defining genetic abnormality), Auer rods (a myeloid blast, never ALL), AML in adults versus ALL in children, and the conditions acute leukemia can grow out of (myelodysplastic syndrome, CML)
ALL, the acute leukemia of young children (usually 1 to 5 years old, a poor prognosis under 1): B-ALL most often, and T-ALL, confirmed as T-cell by testing rather than by its look

Chronic myeloid leukemia, the chronic leukemia he said to know: BCR-ABL1 and the Philadelphia chromosome, a very high count with every stage of maturation and few blasts, chronic versus blast phase, imatinib

CLL/SLL: one disease of small, mature B cells, named by where it is (blood or node); soccer-ball chromatin and smudge cells; at least 5 times 10 to the 9th B cells per liter for CLL, below that monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis; older patients, infections, largely incurable
Burkitt lymphoma: very aggressive and very fast-growing, t(8;14) and MYC, the starry sky of macrophages eating debris, the jaw, EBV, and excellent survival with chemotherapy
Mantle cell lymphoma: from the follicle's mantle zone, t(11;14) (nothing else among the lymphomas carries it), the cyclin D1 stain, older adults with enlarged nodes, survival much longer than it was

Mycosis fungoides, the most common skin lymphoma, an indolent T-cell lymphoma (patches, then plaques, then tumors), and Sézary syndrome, its aggressive form (erythroderma, nodes and cerebriform Sézary cells in the blood)

The other B-cell lymphomas and their associations: follicular lymphoma's t(14;18) and BCL2, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (about 30 percent, de novo or transformed), and marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, the one dentists will see most, with its infections and autoimmune links

The two acute leukemias he said you need: acute promyelocytic leukemia (t(15;17) PML-RARA, maturation stopped at the promyelocyte, DIC, cured by all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide) and acute monocytic leukemia, which can show in the gums
The other T- and NK-cell lymphomas: peripheral T-cell lymphoma (very aggressive, B symptoms, a poor response to chemotherapy) and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (EBV, necrosis, a perforated palate)
Lymphoma categories, his closing point: which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are indolent and which aggressive, and the part of the follicle each B-cell lymphoma comes from

Diagnosing lymphoma: the tissue makes the diagnosis (the B symptoms, high-yield clues, only raise the suspicion); an effaced node; flow cytometry shows the lineage and, with only kappa or only lambda, a clonal population; staging, with disseminated disease as stage 4
Plasma cell neoplasms: a solitary plasmacytoma versus multifocal myeloma in the marrow, rouleaux from the excess antibody, the M-spike, lytic bone, high calcium, kidney damage and anemia (CRAB)

Cryptorchidism, a testis hidden outside the scrotum: the testes descend from the retroperitoneum through the inguinal canal; body heat halts spermatogenesis, so infertility and testicular cancer; surgery if it hasn't come down by the second year prevents the infertility, but the cancer risk stays; the slide: about 3 percent of full-term and 30 percent of premature boys, with torsion and inguinal hernia among its complications

The categories of testicular tumors: 95 percent are germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia, cured in more than 95 percent; the rest are sex cord-stromal tumors (Sertoli and Leydig cells) or mixed, with lymphoma (secondary) and metastases in older men; the slide adds a peak in the 20s and, besides cryptorchidism, a prior testicular cancer and a family history

Seminoma versus the non-seminomatous germ cell tumors: seminoma is the most frequent, in young adults, white and solid without hemorrhage or necrosis, tied to cryptorchidism, usually without a serum marker, and radiosensitive; embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma and teratoma are more aggressive and don't respond as well

Prostatic adenocarcinoma and Gleason grading: the most frequent cancer in men, over 65, in the peripheral zone (no early obstruction), found by serum PSA (which also follows it after treatment), with osteoblastic bone metastases; Gleason runs from well-differentiated glands to masses and single cells, and worse is worse

Benign prostatic hyperplasia: hyperplasia of the glands and stroma around the urethra (the transition zone), in nearly every man after 50, which obstructs the urine; hormones play a role, and surgery treats severe obstruction

The common infections of the male tract: the glans and foreskin, balanoposthitis (nonspecific bacterial, or syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia), epididymitis (usually a spreading urinary tract infection or prostatitis; gonorrhea and chlamydia under 35), and orchitis, which is uncommon (mumps, syphilis, tuberculosis, brucellosis)

HPV and the penis, the lecture's "remember": types 6 and 11 cause condyloma acuminatum, benign and verrucous; types 16 and 18 cause penile intraepithelial neoplasia, flat and red, in younger men, about 30 percent invasive if untreated; the HPV-independent kind, in older uncircumcised men with lichen sclerosus, about 2 to 8 percent

Phimosis and carcinoma of the penis, the closing review: a foreskin that can't retract fills with smegma, then infection, chronic inflammation and carcinoma; penile squamous cell carcinoma is rare in the United States, tied to poor hygiene, indolent, and spreads to the inguinal nodes

Urothelial carcinoma: 90 percent of urinary tract tumors, most in the bladder, in adult men, with minimal painless hematuria; smoking is the strongest risk (four times, and quitting doesn't lower it), with dyes, pelvic radiation, cyclophosphamide and catheters; Schistosoma haematobium causes squamous cell carcinoma; a low-grade papillary carcinoma recurs and rarely invades but can turn high grade, and a high-grade one recurs and can invade

The two emergencies of the testis: torsion (a twisted spermatic cord, intensely painful: the veins close first, then a hemorrhagic infarct of the testis) and inguinal hernia (bowel trapped in an open inguinal canal can infarct; bowel sounds over the mass)

HPV and cervical neoplasia: cancer arises in the transformation zone, where the glandular and squamous epithelia "fight" and stay inflamed and open to HPV; the precursors are squamous intraepithelial lesions, low grade (CIN1, can regress) or high grade (CIN2 and CIN3, progress), about 90 percent HPV-linked (and more than 90 percent of cervical cancers), marked by the koilocyte, in situ until they invade the stroma

Lichen sclerosus, where the lecture paused "because this is important": an atrophic epithelium over dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, a parchment-like vulva; the non-infectious inflammatory disorder the lecture said leads to carcinoma, the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of older women (her slide lists lichen planus beside it); the HPV-associated kind is HPV 16 in more than 70 percent

Infectious vaginitis: Candida (pseudohyphae, little sticks, a lot of inflammation) and Trichomonas vaginalis (a sexually transmitted protozoan that looks like a squamous cell with prolongations), against non-infectious atrophic vaginitis in older women
Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types; benign, finger-like and wart-like, with koilocytes, anywhere on the anogenital tract; less common since the HPV vaccine

The age patterns of the tumors: sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) in girls under 5, with a good prognosis if treated in time; squamous cell carcinomas in women of reproductive age; the HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma and the aggressive serous and clear cell endometrial carcinomas in older women (70 to 80 on the slide)

The common disorders of the vulva, and neoplastic versus non-neoplastic: lichen simplex chronicus (thickened, leathery, from scratching), lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are inflammatory; squamous intraepithelial lesions, VaIN, squamous cell carcinoma, clear cell adenocarcinoma and sarcoma botryoides are neoplastic

Lichen planus, "because you're going to be dentists": vulvar and oral erosions together, with a white, lace-like pattern; a band of lymphocytes under the epithelium; a fresh biopsy (not formalin) for immunofluorescence, which shows shaggy fibrin at the dermoepidermal junction; steroids

Cervical cancer and its prevention: fourth in women worldwide (breast is first), less common in the United States thanks to Pap screening (a fourth of women lack access), the HPV vaccine (decades to show its full benefit), and management now based on each patient's risk; over a lifetime up to 5 percent of unscreened women develop it, under 0.5 percent with screening and treatment

The two endometrial carcinomas, "just know": endometrioid adenocarcinoma (estrogen excess, obesity, estrogen without progesterone; well differentiated, less aggressive, younger women) and the aggressive serous and clear cell carcinomas of women over 65 (70 to 80 on the slide), not hormone-related; endometrioid arises in hyperplasia with atypia

Breast carcinoma: DCIS needs treatment, LCIS is now considered benign; invasive ductal carcinoma forms glands, invasive lobular grows in single files; Paget disease of the nipple means a carcinoma underneath; the prognosis rests on size, nodes and the estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2; of the benign lesions, atypical ductal hyperplasia carries the most risk

Chronic endometritis and the leiomyoma: plasma cells in the endometrium, a common cause of infertility treated with antibiotics; the leiomyoma, very common, a well-circumscribed nodule that makes the uterus bleed, against the aggressive leiomyosarcoma that spreads to the lung; the leiomyosarcoma is infiltrative, with increased mitoses, atypia or necrosis

The ovary and the male breast: most ovarian tumors are epithelial, and ovarian cancer is lethal; gynecomastia (aromatase in fat, testosterone in weightlifters) is far more common than male breast cancer, which has no screening; stage for stage, a man's breast cancer has the same prognosis as a woman's (BRCA2 in some)

podcast.title: Heme & Endo Exam 3: the last-minute review
podcast.blurb: 52 min with Timmy Tooth: Dr. Taylor's Lecture A and L17-L22, each lecture opening on Dr. Herr's study guide, what the professors said to know and to skip, the leukemias on their two axes and the five translocations, and a lightning round to finish.
